class-11/mathematics/calculus/limits.centralConcept: Limits — the value a function approaches

subtopics.name: Definition
points: The limit of f(x) as x tends to a is L if f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a
x approaches a but never needs to equal a
The function may be undefined at a and still have a limit there

subtopics.name: One-sided limits
points: Left-hand limit uses x approaching from below a
Right-hand limit uses x approaching from above a
The two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal

subtopics.name: Algebraic methods
points: Direct substitution first — if it gives a finite value, that is the limit
Factorisation and cancellation for 0/0 forms
Rationalisation for limits involving square roots

subtopics.name: Standard limits
points: lim (x to 0) sin x / x = 1
lim (x to 0) (e^x - 1)/x = 1 and lim (x to 0) log(1+x)/x = 1
lim (x to 0) (a^x - 1)/x = log a

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: indeterminate forms and techniques

subtopics.name: The seven indeterminate forms
points: 0/0, infinity/infinity, 0 x infinity, infinity - infinity
1^infinity, 0^0, infinity^0
Each requires a specific technique, not substitution

subtopics.name: Advanced tools
points: L'Hopital's rule for 0/0 and infinity/infinity forms
Expansion (Taylor or binomial) for small x
For 1^infinity use the exponential limit form: take log first

subtopics.name: Frequently missed
points: A limit existing does not mean the function is continuous there
Left and right limits must agree — checking only one is the commonest error
Do not apply L'Hopital's rule before confirming the form is indeterminate

subtopics.name: Notation and meaning
points: lim x to a f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a
The value f(a) itself is irrelevant to the limit
Limits describe behaviour near a point, not at it

subtopics.name: Existence
points: Limit exists only when left and right limits are equal
A jump discontinuity gives unequal one-sided limits, so no limit exists
Infinite limits describe vertical asymptotes

subtopics.name: Algebra of limits
points: Limit of a sum equals the sum of limits, provided both exist
Same for difference, product and quotient (quotient requires non-zero denominator limit)
Limit of a constant multiple equals the constant times the limit

subtopics.name: Limits at infinity
points: Divide by the highest power of x to evaluate rational functions at infinity
Degree of numerator less than denominator gives limit 0
Equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients

class-11/mathematics/calculus/continuity.centralConcept: Continuity — no breaks in the graph

subtopics.name: Definition at a point
points: f(a) must be defined
lim x to a f(x) must exist
The limit must equal f(a)

subtopics.name: All three are required
points: Failing any one condition makes the function discontinuous at a
A removable discontinuity fails only the third condition
Continuity on an interval means continuity at every point of it

subtopics.name: Removable
points: The limit exists but does not equal f(a), or f(a) is undefined
Graph has a hole at that point
Can be fixed by redefining the function at that single point

subtopics.name: Jump
points: Left and right limits both exist but are unequal
Graph has a visible break
Cannot be removed by redefining one point

subtopics.name: Infinite
points: The function tends to infinity at the point
Vertical asymptote in the graph
Also called an essential discontinuity

subtopics.name: Theorems that need continuity
points: Intermediate value theorem: a continuous function takes every value between f(a) and f(b)
Extreme value theorem: a continuous function on a closed interval attains its maximum and minimum
Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability

subtopics.name: Standard counterexample
points: f(x) = |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there
This is the standard example for the one-way implication
Weierstrass functions are continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere

subtopics.name: Why classify
points: The type of discontinuity determines whether it can be repaired
Classification follows from the behaviour of the one-sided limits
Three main types: removable, jump, infinite

subtopics.name: The three types
points: Removable: limit exists, value differs or is missing — a hole
Jump: both one-sided limits finite but unequal — a step
Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is infinite — an asymptote

subtopics.name: Testing procedure
points: Compute the left-hand limit
Compute the right-hand limit
Compare both with f(a) and classify from the pattern

subtopics.name: Examples
points: (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) at x = 1 is removable — limit 2, value undefined
The sign function at 0 is a jump discontinuity
1/x at 0 is an infinite discontinuity

subtopics.name: Visual signatures
points: A hole means removable discontinuity
A break with a vertical gap means jump discontinuity
A vertical asymptote means infinite discontinuity

subtopics.name: Reading the graph
points: Trace from the left and from the right separately
Note whether the two traces meet, miss, or diverge
Check whether a solid dot fills the gap

subtopics.name: Piecewise functions
points: Piecewise definitions are the commonest source of jumps
Check the boundary point of each piece
Continuity at the boundary requires matching one-sided limits

subtopics.name: Graph to formula
points: A graph with a hole suggests a cancelled common factor
A vertical asymptote suggests a zero in the denominator
A jump suggests a piecewise definition with mismatched pieces

subtopics.name: First principles
points: f'(x) = lim (h to 0) [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h
The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change
It is the limit of the difference quotient

subtopics.name: Geometric meaning
points: The derivative is the slope of the tangent at a point
The secant slope approaches the tangent slope as h tends to 0
f'(a) is the gradient of the curve at x = a

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: differentiation from first principles

subtopics.name: The standard procedure
points: Write f(x+h), expand, subtract f(x)
Divide by h and simplify to remove the h in the denominator
Take the limit as h tends to 0

subtopics.name: Key results
points: d/dx (x^n) = n x^(n-1)
d/dx (sin x) = cos x, d/dx (cos x) = -sin x
d/dx (e^x) = e^x, d/dx (log x) = 1/x

subtopics.name: Differentiability
points: Differentiable at a point requires the limit of the difference quotient to exist
Differentiability implies continuity, not the reverse
Corners, cusps and vertical tangents are points of non-differentiability

subtopics.name: Notation
points: f'(x), dy/dx, and Df(x) all denote the derivative
Leibniz notation dy/dx emphasises the ratio of small changes
Newton's dot notation is used for time derivatives

class-11/mathematics/calculus/rules-of-d.centralConcept: Rules for differentiating combinations of functions

subtopics.name: Power and constant rules
points: d/dx (x^n) = n x^(n-1) for any real n
Derivative of a constant is zero
Derivative of a constant multiple is the constant times the derivative

subtopics.name: Sum and difference
points: The derivative of a sum is the sum of derivatives
Same for difference
Differentiation is linear

subtopics.name: Product rule
points: d/dx (uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx
First times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first
Extends to three factors by repeated application

subtopics.name: Quotient rule
points: d/dx (u/v) = (v du/dx - u dv/dx) / v^2
Order matters — reversing the numerator sign is the classic error
Memory aid: low d-high minus high d-low over low squared

subtopics.name: Chain rule
points: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) x g'(x)
Differentiate the outside, keep the inside, multiply by the inside's derivative
The most used rule in the whole course

subtopics.name: Standard derivatives to memorise
points: d/dx (tan x) = sec^2 x, d/dx (cot x) = -cosec^2 x
d/dx (sec x) = sec x tan x, d/dx (cosec x) = -cosec x cot x

subtopics.name: Logarithmic differentiation
points: Take log of both sides before differentiating when the function is a variable power
Essential for f(x)^g(x) forms
Also simplifies long products and quotients

subtopics.name: Parametric form
points: x and y are both given in terms of a parameter t
dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt)
Requires dx/dt to be non-zero

subtopics.name: Implicit form
points: The relation between x and y is not solved for y
Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x
Collect dy/dx terms and solve

subtopics.name: Worked patterns
points: x = a cos t, y = a sin t gives dy/dx = -cot t
x^2 + y^2 = a^2 gives dy/dx = -x/y
Always apply the chain rule to y terms when differentiating implicitly

subtopics.name: Second derivatives
points: For parametric, d2y/dx2 = (d/dt of dy/dx) / (dx/dt)
For implicit, differentiate dy/dx again and substitute
Second derivatives are where most marks are lost

subtopics.name: Choosing the method
points: Parametric when both coordinates come from a parameter — circles, ellipses, cycloids
Implicit when solving for y is awkward or impossible
Logarithmic when the function is a variable power

subtopics.name: Notation
points: Second derivative written f''(x) or d2y/dx2
nth derivative written f^(n)(x) or dny/dxn
Each differentiation is applied to the previous result

subtopics.name: Physical interpretation
points: First derivative of displacement is velocity
Second derivative is acceleration
Third derivative is jerk

subtopics.name: Geometric interpretation
points: Second derivative gives concavity
Positive means concave up, negative means concave down
Zero with a sign change marks a point of inflection

subtopics.name: Standard nth derivatives
points: d^n/dx^n (x^m) = m!/(m-n)! x^(m-n)
d^n/dx^n (e^ax) = a^n e^ax
d^n/dx^n (sin x) = sin(x + n pi/2)

subtopics.name: Leibniz theorem
points: Gives the nth derivative of a product as a binomial expansion of derivatives
Useful when one factor is a polynomial that eventually differentiates to zero
Reduces long repeated differentiation to one formula

class-11/mathematics/calculus/geometric-.centralConcept: The derivative as slope and rate

subtopics.name: Tangent slope
points: f'(a) is the slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at x = a
Tangent equation: y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a)
Normal is perpendicular, with slope -1/f'(a)

subtopics.name: Rates of change
points: dy/dx measures how fast y changes with x
Related rates problems chain derivatives through time
Marginal cost and marginal revenue are derivatives in economics

subtopics.name: Increasing and decreasing
points: f'(x) > 0 means the function is increasing
f'(x) < 0 means decreasing
Critical points occur where f'(x) = 0 or is undefined

subtopics.name: Curve sketching
points: First derivative locates turning points and monotonicity
Second derivative locates concavity and inflection
Together they give a complete qualitative picture

subtopics.name: Monotonicity
points: Increasing on an interval if f'(x) > 0 throughout
Decreasing if f'(x) < 0 throughout
Strictly monotonic means never flat

subtopics.name: First derivative test
points: Find critical points where f'(x) = 0
If f' changes from positive to negative, it is a local maximum
If f' changes from negative to positive, it is a local minimum

subtopics.name: Second derivative test
points: At a critical point, f'' < 0 gives a local maximum
f'' > 0 gives a local minimum
f'' = 0 is inconclusive — fall back to the first derivative test

subtopics.name: Global extrema on a closed interval
points: Evaluate f at all critical points inside the interval
Also evaluate f at both endpoints
The largest and smallest of these are the global extrema

subtopics.name: Optimisation problems
points: Express the quantity to be optimised as a function of one variable
Use the constraint to eliminate the second variable
Check that the critical point is a maximum or minimum, and that it lies in the valid domain

subtopics.name: Concavity
points: Concave up when f''(x) > 0 — the curve holds water
Concave down when f''(x) < 0 — the curve spills water
Concavity describes how the slope itself is changing

subtopics.name: Points of inflection
points: A point where concavity changes sign
Necessary condition: f''(x) = 0 or undefined
Must verify the sign of f'' actually changes across the point

subtopics.name: Testing
points: Find where f''(x) = 0
Test the sign of f'' on each side
A sign change confirms an inflection; no change means it is not one

subtopics.name: Traps
points: f''(x) = 0 does NOT guarantee an inflection — f(x) = x^4 at 0 is the standard counterexample
An inflection point need not be a stationary point
Concavity and monotonicity are independent properties

subtopics.name: The indefinite integral
points: Integration reverses differentiation
Integral of f(x) dx is F(x) + C where F'(x) = f(x)
The constant C is essential — infinitely many antiderivatives exist

subtopics.name: Standard integrals
points: Integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not equal to -1
Integral of 1/x dx = log|x| + C
Integral of e^x dx = e^x + C

subtopics.name: Substitution
points: Choose u so that du appears in the integrand
Rewrite the whole integral in terms of u
Always convert back to the original variable for indefinite integrals

subtopics.name: By parts
points: Integral of u dv = uv - integral of v du
Choose u by the ILATE order: inverse trig, log, algebraic, trig, exponential
Works when the integrand is a product of unlike functions

subtopics.name: Partial fractions
points: Decompose a rational function before integrating
Distinct linear factors, repeated factors and quadratic factors each have a standard form
Reduces complex rational integrals to logs and arctangents

subtopics.name: Choosing a technique
points: Look for a function and its derivative — substitution
Look for a product of unlike types — by parts
Look for a rational function — partial fractions

subtopics.name: Definition
points: The definite integral from a to b is the limit of a sum of areas of thin rectangles
Written as integral from a to b of f(x) dx
It is a number, not a function — no constant of integration

subtopics.name: Fundamental theorem
points: If F is an antiderivative of f, the definite integral equals F(b) - F(a)
This links area to anti-differentiation
It is the central result of calculus

subtopics.name: Key properties
points: Integral from a to b equals negative of integral from b to a
Integral from a to a is zero
Integral splits at an intermediate point: a to b plus b to c equals a to c

subtopics.name: Symmetry shortcuts
points: For an odd function, the integral over a symmetric interval is zero
For an even function, it doubles the integral from 0 to a
Always check symmetry before computing

subtopics.name: Signed area
points: Area below the x-axis counts as negative
For total geometric area, split at the zeros and take absolute values
This distinction is a standard exam trap

subtopics.name: Approximation
points: Trapezoidal rule and Simpson's rule approximate numerically
Used when no elementary antiderivative exists
Accuracy improves with more subintervals

subtopics.name: The basic result
points: Area between y = f(x), the x-axis, and x = a to x = b is the definite integral of f
Assumes f(x) is non-negative on the interval
Unit of area is the product of the axis units

subtopics.name: When f is negative
points: The integral gives signed area, which may be negative
For geometric area, integrate the absolute value
Split the interval at the x-intercepts

subtopics.name: Area with respect to y
points: Integrate x dy when the curve is easier to express as x = g(y)
Choose the axis that avoids splitting the region
The two approaches must give the same area

subtopics.name: Standard procedure
points: Sketch the region first — most errors are setup errors
Find intersection points to get the limits
Decide which curve is upper and integrate upper minus lower

subtopics.name: The formula
points: Area = integral from a to b of (upper curve - lower curve) dx
a and b are the x-coordinates of the intersection points
Subtracting handles the case where both curves are below the axis

subtopics.name: Finding the limits
points: Set the two equations equal and solve for x
Intersection points give the integration limits
If curves cross inside the interval, split the integral there

subtopics.name: Which curve is upper
points: Test a point between the intersections
The larger y-value at that test point belongs to the upper curve
Getting this backwards gives a negative area

subtopics.name: Choosing the variable
points: If the region is bounded left and right by curves, integrate with respect to y
Right minus left when integrating dy
Picking the wrong variable can force an unnecessary split

subtopics.name: Common exam shapes
points: Line and parabola, circle and line, two parabolas
Symmetry often halves the work
Always sketch — the sketch is worth marks on its own

class-11/mathematics/analytic-geometry/s.centralConcept: Perpendicular distance and angle bisectors of lines

subtopics.name: Perpendicular distance
points: Distance from (x1, y1) to ax + by + c = 0 is |ax1 + by1 + c| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
The absolute value ensures a positive distance
Distance between parallel lines ax+by+c1=0 and ax+by+c2=0 is |c1-c2|/sqrt(a^2+b^2)

subtopics.name: Bisectors of two lines
points: For lines a1x+b1y+c1=0 and a2x+b2y+c2=0, the bisectors are (a1x+b1y+c1)/sqrt(a1^2+b1^2) = ±(a2x+b2y+c2)/sqrt(a2^2+b2^2)
The two signs give the two bisectors, which are perpendicular to each other
The bisector of the acute angle is the one nearer the origin for lines with positive constants

subtopics.name: Identifying acute versus obtuse
points: Compute a1a2 + b1b2; if positive the angle between lines is acute
The sign rule then selects which bisector is the acute one
This is where most marks are lost

subtopics.name: Applications
points: Finding the incentre of a triangle from two bisectors
Locating points equidistant from two lines
Reflection of a point in a line uses the perpendicular foot

class-11/mathematics/analytic-geometry/p.centralConcept: Pair of straight lines from a second-degree equation

subtopics.name: General second-degree equation
points: ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0
Represents a pair of straight lines when a specific condition holds
The condition is abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0

subtopics.name: Homogeneous equation
points: ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 always represents two lines through the origin
Divide by x^2 to get a quadratic in (y/x)
The two roots are the slopes of the two lines

subtopics.name: Angle between the lines
points: tan(theta) = 2 sqrt(h^2 - ab) / (a + b)
Lines are perpendicular when a + b = 0
Lines are coincident when h^2 = ab

subtopics.name: Bisectors and combined properties
points: The bisectors of a homogeneous pair are given by h(x^2 - y^2) = (a - b)xy
Sum and product of slopes come from the quadratic in y/x
The non-homogeneous case factorises into two lines not necessarily through the origin

subtopics.name: Exam technique
points: Check the condition for a pair of lines before factorising
Factorise by treating the equation as a quadratic in one variable
Verify by expanding the factorised form back

subtopics.name: The coordinate system
points: Three mutually perpendicular axes x, y, z meeting at the origin
A point is written as an ordered triple (x, y, z)
The eight octants correspond to the sign combinations

subtopics.name: Distance formula
points: Distance between two points is sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2 + (z2-z1)^2)
Distance from origin is sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)
Direct extension of the two-dimensional formula

subtopics.name: Direction cosines
points: Direction cosines are cos alpha, cos beta, cos gamma, the cosines of angles with the axes
They satisfy cos^2 alpha + cos^2 beta + cos^2 gamma = 1
Direction ratios are any three numbers proportional to the direction cosines

subtopics.name: Section formula
points: Point dividing a segment in ratio m:n has coordinates (mx2+nx1)/(m+n) and similarly for y and z
Midpoint is the special case m = n
External division uses m:n with a minus sign in the denominator

subtopics.name: Centroid and applications
points: Centroid of a triangle is the average of the three vertex coordinates
Direction cosines normalise direction ratios by dividing by their magnitude
These tools underpin the vector treatment of three-dimensional geometry
